❖ Question 7
UID: N8FRI

In a graph with 10 vertices and 15 edges, if the graph is disconnected, what is the maximum possible number of vertices in the largest connected component?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

To make the graph disconnected, we must have at least two components. To maximize one, we minimize the other (1 vertex). If one component has 1 vertex and 0 edges, the other 9 vertices must accommodate all 15 edges.

Max edges in a 9-vertex graph is (9 × 8)/2 = 36. Since 15 ≤ 36, it is possible for 9 vertices to have 15 edges and be connected.

❖ Question 9
UID: K24ZN

Consider the Insertion Sort procedure given below, which sorts an array L of size n(≥2) in ascending order:

begin    

   for xindex:= 2 to n do       

       x := L [xindex];

       j:= xindex - 1;

       while j > 0 and L[j] > x do

           L[j + 1]:= L[j];

           j:= j - 1;

       end {while}

       L [j + 1]:=X;

   end{for}

end

 

It is known that insertion sort makes at most n(n−1)/2 comparisons. Which of the following is true?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

There is no input on which insertion sort makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons.

2

Insertion Sort makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons when the input is already sorted in ascending order.

3

Insertion Sort makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons only when the input is sorted in descending order.

4
✓ Correct Answer

There are more than one input orderings where insertion sort makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons.

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation

In the worst case, the number of comparisons for given Insertion Sort are n(n−1)/2.


Consider the set of numbers 1,2,3,4,5. Some examples for which the number of comparisons are maximum are

  1. Descending order: 5,4,3,2,1
  2.  3,5,4,2,1
  3. 3,5,4,1,2

There is more than 1 sequence for which the number of comparisons is maximum.


  • Insertion sort performs n(n−1)/ 2 comparisons when each new element must be compared against every previously sorted element before finding its place i.e., the inner while loop runs the maximum times.
  • While the descending order (e.g., 5, 4, 3, 2, 1) is a classic worst-case example, it's not the only one.
  • For instance, permutations like 3, 5, 4, 2, 1 or 3, 5, 4, 1, 2 also trigger the full worst-case behavior .

It’s not an exclusive case, thus Option D is the correct one.

❖ Question 16
UID: GSO8E

A text contains characters {A, B, C, D}. The Huffman codewords are A: 0, B: 10, C: 110, D: 111. If the total number of bits in the encoded message is 200 and the character A appears 60 times, what is the maximum possible number of times D could have appeared?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation
  • Total bits L = fA(1) + fB(2) + fC(3) + fD(3) = 200.
  • 60(1) + 2fB + 3fC + 3fD = 200 => 2fB + 3(fC + fD) = 140.
  • To maximize fD, we need to minimize fB and fC.
  • Constraint of Huffman: Frequencies must justify the tree. For A (length 1) to be at depth 1, its frequency must be ≥the combined frequency of others. 60 ≥ fB + fC + fD.
  • Also, fB ≥ fC + fD (since B is at depth 2 while C, D are at depth 3).
  • Let fC = 1 (minimum possible).
  • 2fB + 3(1 + fD) = 140 => 2fB + 3fD = 137.
  • From fB ≥ fC + fD => fB ≥ 1 + fD.
  • Substitute fB = 1 + fD: 2(1 + fD) + 3fD = 137 => 5fD = 135 => fD = 27.
  • Check constraints: If fD = 27, fC = 1, then fB must be at least 27+1 = 28.
  • Total fB+fC+fD = 28+1+27 = 56. 60 ≥ 56 (Satisfied).
  • Max fD = 27.

In an undirected graph G, the number of vertices is 120, and the number of edges is 350. The total weight of a minimum spanning tree (MST) of G is 720. If the weight of each edge in the graph is increased by 4, what will be the new weight of the minimum spanning tree?

?Correct option not available

❖ Question 27
UID: RG9VP

Consider a set of n items with profits P = {p1, p2, ....., pn and weights W = {w1, w2, ....., wn. If all items have the same profit-to-weight ratio pi/wi = k for all i, which of the following is true for the Fractional Knapsack problem?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Any greedy strategy (by max profit, min weight, or ratio) yields the same unique optimal solution.

2
✓ Correct Answer

There may be multiple optimal solutions, but the total profit is always unique.

3

The greedy strategy based on minimum weight is the only one guaranteed to be optimal.

4

The problem reduces to a 0/1 Knapsack problem because the ratios are tied.

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

Solution:

When ratios are identical, the "greedy" choice doesn't distinguish between items.

  • Step 1: Since pi/wi = k, any combination of items that fills the capacity W will yield a profit of k× W.
  • Step 2: One could fill the bag with Item A first or Item B first; while the set of fractions might differ (multiple solutions), the total profit  will always equal k.W (assuming the sum of all weights ≥ W).
  • Why others are incorrect: (A) is wrong because the solution (the set of xi) isn't unique. (C) is wrong because any order works. (D) is wrong because you can still take fractions.

❖ Question 30
UID: 7HULF

Let (S, ≤) be a Poset represented by a Hasse Diagram. Which of the following statements is/are true?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

If the Hasse Diagram is a single path, the Poset is a Total Order.

2

A Hasse Diagram never contains cycles.

3
✓ Correct Answer

Every finite Poset has at least one maximal element.

4
✓ Correct Answer

The relation ≤ is always reflexive, even though loops are not drawn in the Hasse Diagram.

✓ Correct option: 1, 3, 4
💡 View Explanation

1.   A: A total order (or chain) means every pair of elements is comparable, which forms a single vertical path. (True)

2.   B: While Hasse diagrams don't show cycles directly (due to transitivity and antisymmetry), the underlying graph of the diagram (ignoring direction) can have cycles (e.g., the Diamond Lattice M3). (False)

3.   C: In any finite Poset, you can always find an element x such that no y exists where x < y. (True)

4.   D: By convention, Hasse diagrams omit reflexive loops and transitive edges to maintain clarity. (True)

❖ Question 47
UID: 1V9NA

You are running Dijkstra’s algorithm on a directed graph G=(V, E) starting from source s. The graph contains a single edge (u, v) with a negative weight, but no negative cycles. Which of the following is true?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Dijkstra’s algorithm is guaranteed to find the shortest path as long as there are no negative cycles.

2
✓ Correct Answer

Dijkstra’s algorithm may fail because the "Greedy Choice Property" is violated when a shorter path to a "settled" node is discovered later.

3

Dijkstra’s algorithm will work correctly if we add a large constant C to all edge weights to make them positive.

4

The algorithm will enter an infinite loop.

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation
  • Step 1: Dijkstra’s assumes that once a vertex v is extracted from the priority queue (settled), its shortest path distance d[v] is finalized.
  • Step 2: A negative edge can allow a path discovered later to have a smaller sum than the path discovered earlier, breaking the monotonicity requirement.
  • Why others are incorrect: (A) describes Bellman-Ford, not Dijkstra. (C) is a common misconception; adding a constant C penalizes paths with more edges more heavily, potentially changing the shortest path. (D) is wrong; Dijkstra always terminates because it visits each node/edge a finite number of times.

❖ Question 59
UID: 946G5

Which of the following statements is correct regarding Bellman Ford Algorithm?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

We can’t iterate all the edges in any order and relax them.

2
✓ Correct Answer

When a negative weight cycle exists in a graph, every iteration of the cycle will give a shorter path.

3

﻿The Bellman-Ford algorithm always runs faster than Dijkstra's algorithm on graphs with non-negative weights.

4

Bellman-Ford Algorithm can apply to an undirected graph with a negative edge weight cycle.

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

Statement 1: Incorrect. In the Bellman-Ford algorithm, we can iterate over all the edges in any order during the relaxation process. The important part is that each edge is relaxed V−1 times (where V is the number of vertices) to ensure that the shortest path is found. The order of iteration does not affect the correctness of the algorithm, though it may affect the efficiency slightly in practical implementations.

 

Statement 2: Correct. This statement is true. If there is a negative weight cycle in the graph, continuously iterating through the cycle will keep reducing the path cost, leading to increasingly shorter paths. The Bellman-Ford algorithm can detect the presence of such cycles by performing one additional iteration over all edges. If a shorter path is found in this extra iteration, it indicates a negative weight cycle.

 

Statement 3: Incorrect. The Bellman-Ford algorithm does not always run faster than Dijkstra's algorithm on graphs with non-negative weights. In fact, Dijkstra's algorithm is generally faster for graphs with non-negative weights due to its O(E+Vlogfo⁡V) time complexity when implemented with a priority queue, compared to Bellman-Ford's O(V⋅E) time complexity.

 

Statement 4: Incorrect . While the Bellman-Ford algorithm can be applied to undirected graphs, the presence of a negative weight cycle in an undirected graph means the graph is invalid for shortest path computations. In undirected graphs, a negative weight edge effectively creates a negative weight cycle by forming a two-way path. The Bellman-Ford algorithm is designed for directed graphs with potential negative weights but no negative weight cycles.

❖ Question 60
UID: 7951W

Consider two statements about RANDOMIZED QUICKSORT.

S1: There is some input for which randomized quicksort always runs in O(n2) time.

S2: An adversary can provide randomized quicksort with an input array of length n that forces the algorithm to run in O(nlogn) time on that input.

Choose the correct option (assume distinct elements in input):

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Both statements are correct

2

S1 is correct, S2 but is false

3

S1 is false, but S2 is correct

4
✓ Correct Answer

Both Statements are incorrect

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation

S1: There is some input for which randomized quicksort always runs in O(n²) time.

False

·Randomized QuickSort chooses the pivot randomly.

·So for the same input, different runs of the algorithm may behave differently.

·Hence, there is no fixed input that always leads to O(n²) behavior.

There exists an input for deterministic QuickSort that always leads to O(n²) (like sorted or reverse-sorted array),but not for randomized QuickSort, since the pivot is chosen randomly.

S2: An adversary can provide randomized quicksort with an input array of length n that forces the algorithm to run in O(n log n) time on that input.

False.

For any input, the expected running time of quicksort is O(n lg n), where the expectation is taken over the random choices made by quicksort, independent of the choice of the input.

❖ Question 61
UID: 4TK1O

Online Median Finding: The Online Median problem requires us to add elements to a set and at any time to produce the median of the elements added so far. Let n be the no of elements added till now. What is the time complexity for calculating the median? 

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

2

3
✓ Correct Answer

O (n log n)

4

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

Let the set of elements at a given instance is: {7, 8, 9, 6, 5, 4}.

Initially median =7

Now start maintaining two data structures: Min heap And Max heap

Element smaller than the current median will be added to the max heap and which is greater than the current median, will be added to the min heap.

The main property to create a balance between the Min heap and max heap is to balance the size of both. We use two functions:

Add Element(e), add a new element e to the current set, and

Current Median(), return the median of the current set of elements

At each call on Add Element, either the two heaps have an equal size or one of them has one more element than the other; these two states alternate. So, half the calls on Add Element require only a single Insert. When the heap sizes are not equal, the newly-arrived element either belongs in the heap with fewer elements and we regain balance with a single Insert, or it belongs in the heap with more elements and we rebalance with two Inserts plus a DeleteMin. These two cases have equal probability when inputs are random. In summary, with probability 1/4 we perform the three-operation rebalance, and with probability 3/4 we do a single Insert.

Insert will take a Long time. Hence total time for one element= Time required to manage heap+ Insert when Balanced /when unbalanced

Total time for one element= 1 + log n/ 2 log n

Hence total time= n log n


Answer (C)

❖ Question 67
UID: ZTMBG

Let A and B be two sequences of length m and n respectively, to find the longest common subsequence brute force method is applied. Which of the following is the time complexity for the given senario?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

O(n2m)

2

O(2m)

3

O(n)

4

None of above

✓ Correct option: 1
💡 View Explanation

Algorithm:

1.  Find all subsequences of A.

2. For each subsequence of A we will check whether it is a subsequence of ‘B’.

3. Find the longest among common subsequences.


Analysis:

1.  Step 1 will take O(2m) since with ‘m’ length string there will be nearly O(2m) subsequence possible.

2. Step 2 will take O(n2m), to check one subsequence that whether it is a subsequence of string B it will take O(n) time. So, for the 2m subsequences, it takes O(n2m).

3. Step 3 will take O(2m) since nearly there will be 2m subsequences.

Hence, time complexity = O(2m) + O(n2m) + O(2m)

                    = O(n2m).

❖ Question 69
UID: SL3B3

Which of the following is/are Correct?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

If a depth-first search on a directed graph G = (V, E) produces exactly one back edge, then it is possible to choose an edge e ∈ E such that the graph G0 = (V, E − {e}) is acyclic.

2
✓ Correct Answer

Consider a weighted directed graph G = (V, E, w) and let X be a shortest s-t path for s, t ∈ V . If we double the weight of every edge in the graph, setting w’ (e) = 2w(e) for each e ∈ E, then X will still be a shortest s-t path in (V, E, w’ ).

3

Dijkstra’s algorithm may not terminate if the graph contains negative-weight edges.

4
✓ Correct Answer

Given a graph G = (V, E) with positive edge weights, the Bellman-Ford algorithm and Dijkstra’s algorithm can produce different shortest-path trees despite always producing the same shortest-path weights.

✓ Correct option: 1, 2, 4
💡 View Explanation

A. If a depth-first search on a directed graph G = (V, E) produces exactly one back edge, then it is possible to choose an edge e ∈ E such that the graph G0 = (V, E − {e}) is acyclic. True. Removing the back edge will result in a graph with no back edges, and thus a graph with no cycles (as every graph with at least one cycle has at least one back edge). Notice that a graph can have two cycles but a single back edge, thus removing some edge that disrupts that cycle is insufficient, you have to remove specifically the back edge. For example, in graph G = (V, E) = ({a, b, c}, {(a, b),(b, c),(a, c),(c, a)}), there are two cycles [a, b, c, a] and [a, c, a], but only one back edge (c, a). Removing edge (b, c) disrupts one of the cycles that gave rise to the back edge ([a, b, c, a]), but another cycle remains, [a, c, a].

 

B. Consider a weighted directed graph G = (V, E, w) and let X be a shortest s-t path for s, t ∈ V . If we double the weight of every edge in the graph, setting w 0 (e) = 2w(e) for each e ∈ E, then X will still be a shortest s-t path in (V, E, w0 ). True. Any linear transformation of all weights maintains all relative path lengths, and thus shortest paths will continue to be shortest paths, and more generally all paths will have the same relative ordering. One simple way of thinking about this is unit conversions between kilometers and miles.

 

C. Dijkstra’s algorithm may not terminate if the graph contains negative-weight edges. False. It always terminates after |E| relaxations and |V |+|E| priority queue operations, but may produce incorrect results.

 

D. Given a graph G = (V, E) with positive edge weights, the Bellman-Ford algorithm and Dijkstra’s algorithm can produce different shortest-path trees despite always producing the same shortest-path weights. True. Both algorithms are guaranteed to produce the same shortestpath weight, but if there are multiple shortest paths, Dijkstra’s will choose the shortest path according to the greedy strategy, and Bellman-Ford will choose the shortest path depending on the order of relaxations, and the two shortest path trees may be different.

4

Stable, Out-of place, Anti-adaptive

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

Stable :

Elements with identical values appear in the same order in the output array as they were in the input array.


In-place:

Adaptive:

❖ Question 96
UID: SMJI6

Let A be an array of n = 10 elements. We use the Randomized QuickSort algorithm. What is the maximum possible number of comparisons performed in the worst-case scenario?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

Even in Randomized QuickSort, the "worst-case" refers to the worst possible sequence of random choices made by the generator. The maximum number of comparisons occurs when the pivot always results in the most unbalanced partition (0, n-1).

Number of comparisons = (n-1) + (n-2) + ….. + 1 =  n(n-1)/2.

For n=10, comparisons = {10 × 9}/{2} = 45.

❖ Question 99
UID: U1F33

Consider the following statements:

S1: The first edge added by Kruskal's algorithm can be the last edge added by Prim's algorithm.

S2: In a graph, if one raises the lengths of all edges to the power the minimum spanning tree will stay the same.

Which one of the following is correct with respect to above statements S1 and S2?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Only S1 is correct

2

Only S2 is correct

3
✓ Correct Answer

Both S1 and S2 are correct

4

Both are incorrect

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

S1: The first edge added by Kruskal's algorithm can be the last edge added by Prim's algorithm. True. Since Kruskal adds the globally lightest edge first and Prim adds edges based on connectivity from the starting node, it's entirely possible that an edge added early in Kruskal is only needed at the end of Prim’s execution especially if the edge connects parts of the graph far from the starting node.

 

S2: In a graph, if one raises the lengths of all edges to the power the minimum spanning tree will stay the same. True. The MST algorithms care about relative edge lengths, and raising all edge lengths the 3rd power preserves this relationship.

❖ Question 110
UID: VUMBJ

Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. How many relations on A are both symmetric and anti-symmetric?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

1.   A relation R is symmetric if (a, b) ϵ R ⇒ (b, a) ϵ R.

2.   A relation R is anti-symmetric if (a, b) ϵ R and (b, a) ϵ R ⇒ a = b.

3.   Combining these: if a ≠ b and (a, b) ϵ R, then by symmetry (b, a) ϵ R. But by anti-symmetry, this would mean a=b, a contradiction.

4.   Therefore, no pair (a, b) with a ≠ b can be in R.

5.   The only possible elements in R are the diagonal pairs: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4).

6.   Any subset of these 4 diagonal elements will satisfy both properties.

7.   Number of subsets = 24 = 16.

❖ Question 116
UID: EFCLP

An array A contains n distinct elements. We want to find both the 2nd smallest and the 2nd largest elements. What is the minimum number of comparisons required if n=4?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

To find the max/min of 4 elements:

  1. Compare A[1], A[2] (1 comp). Let's say 1 < 2.
  2. Compare A[3], A[4] (1 comp). Let's say 3 < 4.
  3. Compare winners 2, 4 (1 comp). Let's say 4 is Max.
  4. Compare losers 1, 3 (1 comp). Let's say 1 is Min.

Now we have 1 (Min) and 4 (Max). To find 2nd smallest/largest, we look at elements that lost to the max or won against the min. For n=4, the remaining two elements (2 and 3) are automatically the 2nd smallest and 2nd largest in some order. Total = 4 comparisons.

❖ Question 117
UID: U58SQ

Which of the following properties are TRUE regarding Huffman Coding?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

No codeword is a prefix of any other codeword

2
✓ Correct Answer

The tree produced is always a full binary tree (every internal node has two children).

3
✓ Correct Answer

The symbol with the lowest frequency is always at the maximum depth of the tree.

4

If all frequencies are distinct, the Huffman tree is unique in structure.

✓ Correct option: 1, 2, 3
💡 View Explanation

Solution:

  • (A) True: This is the core prefix-free property.
  • (B) True: The algorithm always combines two nodes into one, ensuring 2 children per internal node.
  • (C) True: By the greedy choice property, the smallest two frequencies are combined first, putting them furthest from the root.
  • (D) False: Even with distinct frequencies, the "left" or "right" assignment of 0 and 1 is arbitrary, and if two sums are equal, the tree structure can vary depending on which "tie" is picked.


❖ Question 118
UID: FFQVO

Given an array A of n distinct integers, a local minimum is defined as an element that is smaller than its neighbours (with boundary elements compared to only one neighbour). For example, in A = [11, 7, 5, 4, 13, 20, 19], the local minima are 4 and 19. While finding the absolute minimum requires Ω(n) time in the worst case, what is the tightest possible time complexity for efficiently finding any one local minimum?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

O(n)

2
✓ Correct Answer

O(log n)

3

O(n log n)

4

O

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

You are given an array A of n distinct integers.

  • A local minimum is defined as:
  • For interior elements: A[i] is a local minimum if A[i] < A[i-1] and A[i] < A[i+1]
  • For boundary elements:
  • A[0] is a local minimum if A[0] < A[1]
  • A[n-1] is a local minimum if A[n-1] < A[n-2]

You are not asked to find the global minimum, just any one local minimum.

Although finding the global minimum needs Ω(n) (you must look at all elements), finding a local minimum can be done more efficiently using binary search.

1. Let low = 0 and high = n - 1


2. While low <= high:

  • Let mid = (low + high) // 2
  • Check if A[mid] is a local minimum:

               If A[mid] is less than both its neighbors (or only one if it’s on a boundary),                 return it.

  • If A[mid-1] < A[mid]: Move to the left half (set high = mid - 1)
  • Else if A[mid+1] < A[mid]: Move to the right half (set low = mid + 1)


3. Continue this process recursively.

This works because in any array with distinct elements, if A[mid] is not a local minimum, at least one of its neighbors is smaller — and hence, there must be a local minimum in that direction.

  • This binary search-based algorithm runs in O(log n) time.

Tightest bound on the time complexity to find a local minimum is Θ(log n), so option B is correct.

❖ Question 120
UID: 9TEPM

Consider the following statements:

S1: To find the shortest path in a graph with negative edge weights, one approach is to add a sufficiently large constant to all edges to make them non-negative, and then apply Dijkstra's algorithm.

S2: In solving the single-source shortest path (SSSP) problem on a graph with only non-negative edge weights, it is essential that at least one edge undergoes relaxation more than once.

Which one of the following is correct with respect to above statements S1 and S2?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Only S1 is correct

2

Only S2 is correct

3

Both S1 and S2 are correct

4
✓ Correct Answer

Both are incorrect

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation

S1: To find the shortest path in a graph with negative edge weights, one approach is to add a sufficiently large constant to all edges to make them non-negative, and then apply Dijkstra's algorithm. False. Adding a constant changes the relative costs of paths depending on the number of edges, so it does not preserve the correct shortest paths. That's why Dijkstra’s algorithm cannot be used this way on graphs with negative weights. Instead, algorithms like Bellman-Ford are used for graphs with negative weights.


S2: In solving the single-source shortest path (SSSP) problem on a graph with only non-negative edge weights, it is essential that at least one edge undergoes relaxation more than once. False. Since all edge weights are non-negative, Dijkstra's algorithm can be applied to find the shortest paths, and it guarantees correct results in such cases. In Dijkstra’s algorithm, once an edge is relaxed and its associated vertex is extracted from the priority queue, that vertex (and its edges) are not revisited.

❖ Question 133
UID: O8Z6E

What will be the complexity of applying Huffman coding on n-character where the frequency of character is represented with min heap as a data structure?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

O(n2)

2
✓ Correct Answer

O(nlogn)

3

O(logn2)

4

O(n)

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

1. Time for creating a minimum heap of ‘n’ character frequencies = O(n)

2. Taking the minimum frequency node from min-heap and deleting if from heap = O(logn)

❖ Question 140
UID: 0THSP

Let G be a directed graph that contains negative weight edges, but no negative weight cycles. Consider running Dijkstra’s algorithm on G.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Dijkstra’s algorithm always produces the correct shortest paths since there are no negative cycles

2
✓ Correct Answer

Dijkstra’s algorithm may produce incorrect results on such graphs

3

Dijkstra’s algorithm may fail, but adding a large positive constant to all edge weights will make it work correctly

4

Dijkstra’s algorithm may not terminate in this case.

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

Dijkstra’s algorithm may produce incorrect results on such graphs.

  • Dijkstra’s algorithm assumes that once a node’s shortest distance is found, it won’t change.
  • This assumption fails if negative weight edges are present, even if there are no negative cycles.
  • So, Dijkstra can mark a node’s distance prematurely and miss a shorter path discovered later via a negative edge.

So the new weight of MST is 500 + 495 which is 995.

Answer (C)

❖ Question 155
UID: F3C40

Consider the following Statements:-

S1:In a breadth-first search of an undirected graph, there are no back edges and no forward edges.

S2:In a breadth-first search of a directed graph there are no forward edges.

Number of correct statements is/are __________.

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

Explanation:-

Both statement S1 and S2 are correct because in breadth first search we do searching as level order search. We first search all the adjacent vertices for a given node then we go the next vertex.


statement s1 proof:- Suppose (u, v) is a back edge or a forward edge in a BFS of an undirected graph. Then one of u and v, say u, is a proper ancestor of the other (v) in the breadth-first tree. Since we explore all edges of u before exploring any edges of any of u’s descendants, we must explore the edge (u, v) at the time we explore u. But then (u, v) must be a tree edge.


Statement s2 proof:- Suppose (u, v) is a forward edge. Then we would have explored it while visiting u, and it would have been a tree edge.

Ans. 2 to 2

❖ Question 188
UID: 823UW

In Job Sequencing with Deadlines, where each job takes unit time, suppose we have n jobs and the maximum deadline is D. If we sort jobs in non-increasing order of profits, what is the tightest upper bound on the time complexity to find the optimal sequence using a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) data structure with path compression?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

O(n log n)

2

O(nα(n))

3

O(n log D)

4
✓ Correct Answer

O(n log n + n α(D))

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation

Solution:

  • Step 1: Sorting takes O(n log n).
  • Step 2: For each job, we find the latest available slot using DSU. The DSU is initialized over the range of deadlines [0, D].
  • Step 3: We perform n find and union operations on a set of size D. The complexity of these operations with path compression is O(n α(D)).
  • Total: O(n log n + n α(D)).
  • Why others are incorrect: (A) ignores the DSU overhead; (B) ignores the initial sorting; (C) is the complexity for a standard array-based search.

Consider a directed graph given in below, DFS of the below graph is 1 2 4 6 3 5 7 8. In the diagram below, if DFS is applied on this graph a tree is obtained which is connected using green edges.

Tree Edge: It is an edge which is present in a tree obtained after applying DFS on the graph. All the Green edges are tree edges.

Forward Edge: It is an edge (u, v) such that v is descendant but not part of the DFS tree. Edge from 1 to 8 is a forward edge.

 Cross Edge: It is an edge which connects two nodes such that they do not have any ancestor and a descendant relationship between them. Edge from node 5 to 4 is cross edge.

❖ Question 210
UID: UBD36

In which of the following sorting algorithms is each pair of elements compared at most once during the entire execution of the algorithm?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

Insertion Sort

2

In-place Heap Sort

3
✓ Correct Answer

Merge Sort

4
✓ Correct Answer

In-place Quick Sort

✓ Correct option: 1, 3, 4
💡 View Explanation

Insertion Sort compares one element at a time with the already sorted portion of the array, and each element is only considered for insertion once.


Merge Sort, during its merge step, compares elements only between the two subarrays being merged. Once merged, elements are not compared again with those in their original subarrays.


In-place Quick Sort uses a pivot to partition the array. Each element is compared with the pivot during the partition step, and once placed, that pivot isn't involved in further comparisons.


Heap Sort, on the other hand, may compare the same pair of elements multiple times. This can happen when an element moves (or “percolates”) through the heap during repeated heapify operations.

❖ Question 226
UID: 5Q6EE

In the Fractional Knapsack problem, let S be the solution set. If we increase the capacity of the knapsack by  W, which of the following could happen?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

The total profit increases by at least ∆ W × ({ratio of the last item added}).

2
✓ Correct Answer

An item that was previously not included in S at all may now be partially included.

3
✓ Correct Answer

The relative order of items (by pi/wi) in the optimal solution remains unchanged.

4
✓ Correct Answer

The total profit remains the same if all items were already included in the original S.

✓ Correct option: 2, 3, 4
💡 View Explanation

Solution:

  • (A) False: It increases by exactly ∆ W × ratio, provided that item isn't exhausted. "At least" is incorrect if only low-ratio items remain.
  • (B) True: If the bag was full and a new item was waiting, more capacity allows its inclusion.
  • (C) True: The greedy choice is based on ratios, which are independent of capacity.
  • (D) True: If W already contained all items, more capacity adds no value.

❖ Question 230
UID: BQ78N

Consider the recursive quicksort algorithm with "random pivoting". That is, in each recursive call, a pivot is chosen uniformly at random from the sub-array being sorted. When this randomized algorithm is applied to an array of size n all whose elements are distinct, what is the probability that the smallest and the largest elements in the array are compared during a run of the algorithm?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

2
✓ Correct Answer

3

4

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

The question is asking

What is the probability that the smallest and largest elements are compared during a run of randomized QuickSort?

In randomized Quicksort, a comparison between the smallest and largest elements can only occur if one of them is chosen as the pivot during the first partition.

Why?

  • Suppose the pivot selected in the first split is neither the smallest nor the largest element.
  • Then the smallest element will end up in the left subarray, and the largest in the right subarray.
  • Since QuickSort only compares elements within the same recursive subarray, the smallest and largest will never be compared again they’re now in separate branches.

Therefore, for the smallest and largest elements to be compared, one of them must be chosen as the pivot in the first step.

  • The pivot is selected randomly from the N elements.
  • So, the probability of selecting either the smallest or the largest element as the first pivot is:

Probability= 2/N

❖ Question 238
UID: 38QXK

In a Huffman tree, if the frequencies of n characters are the first n Fibonacci numbers (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, ....., Fn), what is the length of the codeword for the character with frequency Fn?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

1

2

n-1

3

n-2

4

log2 n

✓ Correct option: 1
💡 View Explanation

Fibonacci frequencies create a strictly skewed tree.

  • 1+1 = 2. New set: {2, 2, 3, 5, ..... .
  • 2+2 = 4. New set: {4, 3, 5, ..... →  {3, 4, 5, ..... .
  • 3+4 = 7. New set: {7, 5, ..... →  {5, 7, ..... .

In every step, the sum of all previous frequencies is Fk+2-1, which is always slightly less than or equal to the next Fibonacci number. This keeps the most frequent character (Fn) at the very top level (depth 1).

In a modified version of Quicksort, the pivot is selected as the median of five elements chosen from the array. These five positions are:

  • left (i.e., index 0),
  • right (last index),
  • center (average of left and right, rounded down),
  • leftOfCenter (average of left and center, rounded down), and
  • rightOfCenter (average of right and center, rounded down).

The pivot is chosen as the median among the elements at these five positions.

What is the worst-case time complexity of this Quicksort variant?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

O(n)

2
✓ Correct Answer

O(nlogn)

3

O(n²)

4

O(n²log n)

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation
  • Even though this pivot strategy (median-of-five) generally improves average-case performance by aiming for more balanced partitions, it does not eliminate the possibility of skewed partitions.
  • In the worst case, the array could still be partitioned in a highly unbalanced way—e.g., one side with n−1 elements and the other with 0.
  • This leads to the recurrence:

                    T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n) ⇒ O(n2)

  • So, despite improved pivot selection, worst-case time complexity remains O(n2) unless special pivot selection like median-of-medians is used, which guarantees linear time pivot selection.

❖ Question 279
UID: U99JB

Which of the following is/are False about Minimum spanning Tree?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

A MST contains a cycle

2
✓ Correct Answer

If we remove an edge from a MST, the resulting subgraph is still a MST.

3

If we add an edge to a MST, the resulting subgraph is still a MST

4
✓ Correct Answer

If there are V vertices in a given graph, a MST of that graph contains |V | − 1 edges.

✓ Correct option: 1, 2, 4
💡 View Explanation

(a) A MST contains a cycle. False. Trees (including minimum spanning trees) never contain cycles.


(b) If we remove an edge from a MST, the resulting subgraph is still a MST. False, the set of edges we chose will no longer connect everything to everything else.


(c) If we add an edge to a MST, the resulting subgraph is still a MST. False, an MST on a graph with n vertices always has n − 1 edges.


(d) If there are V vertices in a given graph, a MST of that graph contains |V | − 1 edges. True. This is true (assuming the initial graph is connected).

❖ Question 280
UID: KE967

How many of the following statements is/are TRUE?

(i) Every DAG has exactly one topological ordering.

(ii) If a DFS in an undirected graph G contains exactly one back-edge, then G can be made acyclic by removing one edge.

(iii) If G is a directed graph and can be made acyclic by removing exactly one edge, then any DFS in G will only contain exactly one back-edge.

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

(i) Every DAG has exactly one topological ordering. False Consider the graph {(A, B),(A, C)}, which has two topological orderings ABC and ACB. Some priority constraints may be unspecified, and multiple orderings may be possible for a given DAG. For example a graph G = (V, E) = ({a, b, c}, {(a, b),(a, c)}) has valid topological orderings [a, b, c] or [a, c, b]. As another example, G = (V, E) = ({a, b}, {}) has valid topological orderings [a, b] or [b, c].


(ii) If a DFS in an undirected graph G contains exactly one back-edge, then G can be made acyclic by removing one edge. True Component with back edge remains connected with k − 1 edges where k is number of nodes in that component, so it is a tree and is acyclic.


(iii) If G is a directed graph and can be made acyclic by removing exactly one edge, then any DFS in G will only contain exactly one back-edge. False Two different cycles can share one edge, thus by removing that one edge the entire graph is made acyclic.

Only S2 is correct.

3

Both S1 and S2 is correct

4

Neither S1 nor S2 are correct.

✓ Correct option: 1
💡 View Explanation

S1: If a topological sort exists for the vertices in a directed graph, then a DFS on the graph will produce no back edges. True. Both parts of the statement hold if and only if the graph is acyclic.


S2: Dynamic programming is more closely related to BFS than it is to DFS. False. DFS is more closely related. The top-down approach to dynamic programming is effectively performing DFS on the subproblem dependence graph. The bottom-up approach means solving subproblems in the order of a reverse topological sort, which is also related to DFS.

❖ Question 330
UID: 1RRNW

Which of the following sorting algorithms have a time complexity that remains the same regardless of the nature of the input?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Bubble sort

2

Quick sort

3
✓ Correct Answer

Merge Sort

4

Insertion Sort

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation
  • Merge Sort has a guaranteed time complexity of O(n log n) in all cases (best, average, and worst) because it always divides the array into halves and performs the merge operation systematically.
  • Quick Sort has a worst-case time complexity of O(n²) (e.g., when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element).
  • Bubble Sort and Insertion Sort can run in O(n) time for nearly sorted inputs but degrade to O(n²) in the worst case, so their time complexity depends on input.

Hence, Merge Sort is the only one listed with a guaranteed input-independent time complexity.

❖ Question 346
UID: V64GN

Let G be a connected, weighted undirected graph. If we multiply all edge weights by a positive constant k and then add a constant c > 0 to every edge weight, which of the following remain unchanged?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

The specific edges that form the Minimum Spanning Tree.

2

The specific edges that form the Shortest Path between two nodes u and v.

3
✓ Correct Answer

The order in which Kruskal’s algorithm adds edges to the MST.

4

The order in which Dijkstra’s algorithm relaxes edges from a source s.

✓ Correct option: 1, 3
💡 View Explanation
  • MST (A & C): MSTs depend only on the relative order of edge weights. If w(e1) < w(e2), then k . w(e1) + c < k . w(e2) + c for k > 0. Thus, Kruskal’s picks them in the same order, and the MST remains identical.
  • Shortest Path (B & D): This is different. A path with 2 edges of weight 10 (Total 20) is shorter than a path with 3 edges of weight 7 (Total 21). If we add c=10 to all, the first becomes 20+20=40, and the second becomes 21+30=51. The order holds here, but if c was larger, the path with fewer edges would eventually be favored even if its original weight was higher.

❖ Question 354
UID: OXCCS

For obtaining a minimum spanning tree we have used Kruskal Algorithm. In the Kruskal algorithm when we get the minimum weight edge then we perform cycle checking. Asymptotically what amount of time will be required for cycle checking if there are ‘E’ edges and ‘V’ vertices in the graph:

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

O (V2)

2

O(log V)

3

O (E2)

4
✓ Correct Answer

O (E)

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation

In cycle checking in Kruskal, we perform

1. Find the minimum edge and then take vertices of that edge and then check whether the vertices belong to the same set or not.

2. If vertices belong to the same set then we do not consider that edge because it will make a cycle.

3. If vertices do not belong to the same set then, perform a union of vertices and make a set and accept that edge.

To perform this operation constant time is required because each time there will be only two vertices for which we have to perform union and make a set.

 The time complexity of each cycle checking = O(1)

In the worst case number of cycle, we have to check will be equal to the number of edges.

 Total time for cycle checking = E × 1 = O (E).

Answer (D)

❖ Question 358
UID: 7UP7Q

Consider a weighted undirected graph G where all edge weights are distinct. Let e{max} be the edge with the maximum weight in G. Which of the following statements is always true?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

emax can never be part of any Minimum Spanning Tree (MST).

2

If emax is part of a cycle C, then e{max} cannot be in the MST.

3

emax must be part of the MST if it is incident to a vertex of degree 1.

4
✓ Correct Answer

Both B and C are correct.

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation
  • Step 1 (Cycle Property): In an MST, for any cycle in the graph, the edge with the strictly maximum weight in that cycle cannot belong to the MST. Since all weights are distinct, emax being the heaviest in cycle C guarantees its exclusion.
  • Step 2 (Cut Property): If a vertex has degree 1, the only edge incident to it must be included in the MST to ensure the graph is connected, regardless of its weight.
  • Why others are incorrect: (A) is false because if emax is a bridge (cut-edge), it must be in the MST. (B) and (C) are both mathematically sound properties of MSTs.

❖ Question 390
UID: P9IN5

Let G be a weighted connected undirected graph with distinct positive edge weights. If every edge weight is increased by the same value, then which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Minimum spanning tree of G does not change

2
✓ Correct Answer

Shortest path between any pair of vertices does not change

3
✓ Correct Answer

Kruskal's algorithm is considered a Greedy Algorithm, while Prim's algorithm is not.

4

Kruskal's algorithm can return different spanning trees for the same input graph G, depending on how it breaks ties when the edges are sorted into order.

✓ Correct option: 2, 3
💡 View Explanation

(A) is true: If we increase the weight of every edge in a graph by the same value, the relative weights of the edges do not change. Therefore, the order of the edges in the sorted list of edges does not change, and the minimum spanning tree (MST) remains the same.

 

(B) is false: If we increase the weight of every edge in a graph by the same value, the shortest path between two vertices may change. For example, consider a graph with three vertices connected by edges with weights 1, 2, and 3. The shortest path between vertices A and C is A-B-C with weight 3. If we increase the weights of all edges by 1, the shortest path between A and C becomes A-C with weight 5.

 

(C) is false. Both Prims and Kruskals are Greedy Algorithms.


(D) is true: Suppose that we wanted to pick T as our minimum spanning tree. Then, to obtain this tree with Kruskal's algorithm, we will order the edges first by their weight, but then will resolve ties in edge weights by picking an edge first if it is contained in the minimum spanning tree, and treating all the edges that aren't in T as being slightly larger, even though they have the same actual weight.


With this ordering, we will still be finding a tree of the same weight as all the minimum spanning trees w(T). However, since we prioritize the edges in T, we have that we will pick them over any other edges that may be in other minimum spanning trees.

❖ Question 391
UID: TK6XE

Which of the following statement is false? 

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

The depth of any DFS (Depth First Search) tree rooted at a vertex is at least as much as the depth of any BFS tree rooted at the same vertex.

2
✓ Correct Answer

if all edges in a graph have distinct weight then the shortest path between two vertices is unique

3

For a directed graph, the absence of back edges in a DFS tree means graph has no cycle

4

  BFS takes  time in a graph G(V,E) if the graph is represented with an adjacency matrix.

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

Statement B. is false

(a) TRUE. Since BFS finds paths using the fewest number of edges, the BFS depth of any vertex is at least as small as the DFS depth of the same vertex. Thus, the DFS tree has a greater or equal depth.

(b) FALSE. Even if no two edges have the same weight, there could be two paths with the same weight. For example, there could be two paths from s to t with lengths 3 + 5 = 8 and 2 + 6 = 8. These paths have the same length (8) even though the edges (2, 3, 5, 6) are all distinct.

(c) TRUE. It is true that the absence of back edges with respect to a DFS tree implies that the graph is acyclic.

(d) TRUE. With an adjacency matrix representation, visiting each vertex takes O(V ) time, as we must check all N possible outgoing edges in the adjacency matrix. Thus, BFS will take O(V 2 ) time using an adjacency matrix.

A. Dijkstra’s – Computes single-source shortest paths. Does not compute all-pairs reachability.

B. Kruskal’s – Used for minimum spanning trees (undirected graphs).

C. Prim’s – Also used for MSTs, not applicable for reachability or directed graphs.

 

Apply Floyd-Warshall algorithm. After this, if the entry in D(n) (i, j) is still ∞, it implied that there is no path from i to j, otherwise, there is some path. Thus E* (i, j) = 1 if D(n) (i, j) ≠∞, 0 otherwise.

The transitive closure of a graph tells us whether a path exists from node i to node j for all pairs of nodes.

The Floyd-Warshall algorithm is a classic dynamic programming approach that computes all-pairs shortest paths in a graph.

Even if we’re not interested in distances, but only reachability (i.e., path exists or not), we can modify Floyd-Warshall to compute transitive closure by using boolean logic instead of weights.

❖ Question 400
UID: 50T6P

Consider an Abstract Data Type (ADT) TripleStack implemented using a single array of size N. Three stacks S1, S2, S3 grow towards each other. S1 starts at index 0, S2 starts at N-1, and S3 starts at N/2 and can grow in either direction. What is the condition for "Stack Full"?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Addr(j, i)

2

Addr(i, j) + (j-i)(n-1)w

3
✓ Correct Answer

AddrRM + (j-i)(n-1)w

4

Addr(n-i, n-j)

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

In Row-Major: AddrRM(i, j) = α + (i . n + j)w.

In Column-Major: AddrCM(i, j) = α + (j . n + i)w.

Subtracting the two: AddrCM - AddrRM = (jn + i - in - j)w = (j(n-1) - i(n-1))w = (j-i)(n-1)w.

Therefore, AddrCM = AddrRM + (j-i)(n-1)w.

S2: Given a connected graph G = (V, E), if a vertex v ∈ V is visited during level k of a breadth-first search from source vertex s ∈ V , then every path from s to v has length at most k.

💡 View Explanation

The adjacency list structure needs to be traversed to find the incoming edges for each vertex. This structure has total size Θ(V + E), so this takes Θ(V + E) time to compute.

❖ Question 408
UID: 9NE19

Consider the following statements:

S1: Suppose we do a DFS on a directed graph G. If we remove all of the back edges found, the resulting graph is now acyclic.

S2: Both DFS and BFS require Ω(V ) storage for their operation. (That is, for working storage, above and beyond the storage needed to represent the input.)

S3: A depth-first search of a directed graph always produces the same number of tree edges (i.e. independent of the order in which the vertices are provided and independent of the order of the adjacency lists).

Which of the following is/are CORRECT?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Only S1 is correct.

2

Both S2 & S3 are correct.

3
✓ Correct Answer

Both S2 & S3 are correct.

4

All S1, S2, & S3 are correct

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

S1: Suppose we do a DFS on a directed graph G. If we remove all of the back edges found, the resulting graph is now acyclic. True. If DFS finds no back edges, then the graph is acyclic. Removing any back edges found doesn’t change the traversal order of DFS, so running DFS again on the modified graph would produce no back edges.


S2: Both DFS and BFS require Ω(V ) storage for their operation. (That is, for working storage, above and beyond the storage needed to represent the input.) True. Each needs to keep track of the vertices that have already been visited.


S3: A depth-first search of a directed graph always produces the same number of tree edges (i.e. independent of the order in which the vertices are provided and independent of the order of the adjacency lists). False. The DFS forest may contain different numbers of trees (and tree edges) depending on the starting vertex and upon the order in which vertices are searched. Consider the example below. If the DFS starts at a, then it will visit b next, and (a, b) will become a tree edge. But if the DFS visits b first, then a and b become separate trees in the DFS forest, and (a, b) becomes a cross edge.

❖ Question 410
UID: DY16Z

Consider the following statements:

S1: The heaviest edge in a graph cannot belong to the minimum spanning tree.


S2: The maximum spanning tree (spanning tree of maximum cost) can be computed by negating the cost of all the edges in the graph and then computing minimum spanning tree.

Which one of the following is correct with respect to above statements S1 and S2?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Only S1 is correct

2
✓ Correct Answer

Only S2 is correct

3

Both S1 and S2 are correct

4

Both are incorrect

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

S1: The heaviest edge in a graph cannot belong to the minimum spanning tree. False. The heaviest edge may or may not be part of the MST it depends on the graph structure. In a graph where the heaviest edge is the only edge connecting two components, it must be in the MST. So, there’s no general rule that the heaviest edge is always excluded from the MST.

 

S2: The maximum spanning tree (spanning tree of maximum cost) can be computed by negating the cost of all the edges in the graph and then computing minimum spanning tree. True. If you negate all edge weights, the lightest edges become heaviest, and vice versa. Computing MST on the negated weights will give the minimum total negative weight, which corresponds to maximum total positive weight in the original graph.

❖ Question 430
UID: 5IDSW

What does the following C program segment do?

int n = arr.size().

int ans = INT_MIN.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

   for (int j = i, curSum = 0; j < n; j++)

   {

        curSum += arr[j].

        ans = (ans > curSum)? ans : curSum;

    }

  }

return ans;

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Calculates the maximum sum within the given array containing both positive and negative integers.

2

Calculates the maximum subarray sum within the given array containing positive integers only.

3
✓ Correct Answer

A more efficient solution to this problem is divide and conquer with O(nlogn) time complexity and O(logn) space complexity.

4

Consider a sequence of 14 elements arr= [-5, -10,6,1, -2,13,9, -1,4,12, -3,0]. The output would be 0.

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

Functionality of the code: We are given an array ‘arr’ and it returns the maximum sum of a subarray in arr. The code works fine for both negative and positive integers. This is a Brute force solution of O(n^2) time complexity. We are calculating sum for every subarray and storing the maximum in ‘ans’

 

We can solve this using divide and conquer strategy. This is the follow-up question asked in this question. This involves modelling the problem by observing that the maximum subarray sum is such that it lies somewhere -

 

entirely in the left-half of array [L, mid-1], OR

entirely in the right-half of array [mid+1, R], OR

in array consisting of mid element along with some part of left-half and some part of right-half such that these form contiguous subarray - [L', R'] = [L', mid-1] + [mid] + [mid+1, R'], where L' >= L and R' <= R

 

Time Complexity    : O(NlogN), the recurrence relation can be written as T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N) since we are recurring for left and right half (2T(N/2)) and also calculating maximal subarray including mid element which takes O(N) to calculate. Solving this recurrence using master theorem, we can get the time complexity as O(NlogN)

 

Space Complexity: O(logN), required by recursive stack

So, the correct option is C.

❖ Question 437
UID: M2FSK

Consider the following statements:-

S1:A directed graph is acyclic if and only if a depth first search yields no “back” edges.

S2:In a depth-first search of an undirected graph G, every edge of G is either a tree edge or a back edge.

Number of correct statement(s) is ______________.

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

Explanation:-

Statement 1 is correct because if we have back edge in depth first search traversal for a directed graph G then G will definitely have cycle in it.

Statement 2 is also correct. Let (u, v) be an arbitrary edge of G, and suppose without loss of generality that u.d < v.d. Then the search must discover and finish ‘v’ before it finishes ‘u’ (while u is grey i.e. exploring vertex), since v is on u’s adjacency list. If the first time that the search explores edge (u, v), it is in the direction from u to v, then v is undiscovered until that time, for otherwise the search would have explored this edge already in the direction from v to u. Thus, (u, v) becomes a tree edge. If the search explores (u, v) is a back edge, since u is still grey at the time the edge is first explored.

Ans. 2 to 2

❖ Question 448
UID: AA4XQ

Given a graph with 5 vertices {A, B, C, D, E}. The number of edges in the graph is 6. If the DFS discovery times d[v] and finish times f[v] are as follows:A(1,10), B(2,9), C(3,4), D(5,8), E(6,7).

How many Back Edges are possible in this DFS tree?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

The structure is: A is root, B is child of A, C and D are children of B, E is child of D.

Total edges in the graph = 6.

Tree edges = n-1 = 4.

Remaining edges = 6 - 4 = 2.

For an edge to be a back edge, it must go from descendant to ancestor.

The nesting is: E ⊂ D ⊂ B ⊂ A and C ⊂ B ⊂ A.

The "extra" edges must be verified. Since C and D are siblings, an edge between them is a cross-edge. Only an edge like (E, B) or (D, A) counts as a back edge. Based on the 6-edge constraint, we have 2 non-tree edges. If the graph is undirected, both are back edges; if directed, we look at intervals. Here, E(6,7) is inside B(2,9). A directed edge (E, B) is a back edge. However, (C, D) is a cross edge because their intervals (3,4) and (5,8) are disjoint. Thus, only 1 back edge is possible if one edge is (C,D).

The question asks how many are possible. Given the tree structure and 6 edges, one edge is (C,D) [cross] and one could be (E,B) [back].

Numerical instability in some floating-point contexts.

❖ Question 500
UID: Z2Z00

How many calls of merge-sort are performed when sorting an array of size 128. Base case is an array containing a single element.

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
?Correct option not available
💡 View Explanation

Merge Sort recursively divides the array into halves until it reaches size 1.

Each call divides the array into two parts and makes two recursive calls. So this builds a binary recursion tree.

Total Merge Sort Calls = Number of Nodes in the Binary Tree

For an array of size n, the recursion tree has:

Total Calls = 2n−1

This includes:

n leaf nodes (base cases where array size = 1)

n – 1 internal calls (actual merge steps)

For n = 128

Total merge sort calls = 2 × 128 – 1= 255

❖ Question 507
UID: EEL9D

Let m[i,j] be the minimum number of scalar multiplication required in order to parenthesis matrix Ai to Aj. So,

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

expr1 = 0 & expr2 = min{m[i,k] + m[k+1, j] + pi-1pkpj} ; i  k < j

2

expr1 = min {m[i,k] + m[k+1, j] + pi-1pkpj} & expr2 = 0 ; i  k < j

3

expr1 = 0 & expr2 = min{m[i,k] + m[k+1, j] + pi-1pkpj} ; i  k  j

4

expr1 = 0 & expr2 = min{m[i,k] + m[k+1, j] + pi-1pkpj} ; i < k  j

✓ Correct option: 1
💡 View Explanation

expr1 =0, because if there is only one matrix, then there will be no multiplication of the matrix.


For expr 2 the following steps will be there:

Step 1: Take the sequence of matrices and separate them into two subsequences.

Step 2: Find the minimum cost of multiplying out each subsequence.

Step 3: Add these costs together and add the cost of multiplying the two resultant matrices.

Step 4: Repeat steps 1, 2, and 3  for each possible position at which the sequence of matrices can be split, and take the minimum for all of these.


By following these steps we will get the recurrence equation as shown below:-

& expr2 = min{m[i,k] + m[k+1, j] + pi-1pkpj} ; i  k < j.

❖ Question 510
UID: TPL9F

Consider the following statements:

S1: For a dynamic programming algorithm, computing all values in a bottom-up fashion is asymptotically faster than using recursion and memoization.

S2: The running time of a dynamic programming algorithm is always Θ(P) where P is the number of subproblems.

Which of the following is/are Correct about statements S1 and S2?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Only S1 is true.

2

Only S2 is true.

3

Both S1 and S2 are correct

4
✓ Correct Answer

Both S1 and S2 are incorrect.

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation

S1: For a dynamic programming algorithm, computing all values in a bottom-up fashion is asymptotically faster than using recursion and memoization. False. A bottom-up implementation must go through all of the subproblems and spend the time per subproblem for each. Using recursion and memoization only spends time on the subproblems that it needs. In fact, the reverse may be true: using recursion and memoization may be asymptotically faster than a bottom-up implementation.


S2: The running time of a dynamic programming algorithm is always Θ(P) where P is the number of subproblems. False. The running time of a dynamic program is the number of subproblems times the time per subproblem. This would only be true if the time per subproblem is O(1).

❖ Question 520
UID: ZADFX

Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Graph Traversal algorithms?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

BFS is used to find the shortest path between two nodes in an unweighted graph.

2

DFS can be implemented using a Stack (either explicitly or via recursion).

3

BFS explores all neighbors of a node before moving to the next level.

4
✓ Correct Answer

DFS always finds the path with the minimum number of edges between two nodes.

✓ Correct option: 4
💡 View Explanation

·Statement D is incorrect: DFS (Depth First Search) follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking. It does not consider other branches until it hits a dead end, meaning the first path it finds to a target might be much longer than the shortest possible path.

·Statement A is correct: Because BFS (Breadth First Search) explores nodes level-by-level (layer-by-layer), the first time it reaches a target node, it is guaranteed to have used the fewest number of edges.

·Statement B and C are correct: These are the standard definitions. BFS uses a Queue (FIFO) to explore neighbors, while DFS uses a Stack (LIFO) to explore depth

In the "Median of Medians" algorithm for selection, we divide the array into groups of 5. If we divided the array into groups of 3 instead, what would the recurrence be?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + O(n)

The algorithm would not necessarily run in linear time.

💡 View Explanation

2

Insertion Sort; O(nk)

3
✓ Correct Answer

HeapSort using a Min-Heap of size k+1; O(n log k)

4

MergeSort; O(n log n)

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

This is a nearly sorted array (k-sorted).

  • Insertion Sort would take O(nk).
  • HeapSort (C): By maintaining a min-heap of the first k+1 elements, the root is guaranteed to be the overall minimum. We extract root and add the next element. Each of n elements involves a log k operation. Total O(n log k).

Since k is usually much smaller than n, O(n log k) is superior.

  4. Merge Degree: In each subsequent pass, we can merge M-1 runs (i.e., 100 runs).

❖ Question 563
UID: 7B4QB

Consider the problem of finding the Majority Element (an element that appears more than n/2 times) in an array of size n. A Divide & Conquer approach divides the array into two halves, finds the majority element in each half, and then combines them. What is the time complexity of this specific D&C approach?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

θ(n)

2
✓ Correct Answer

θ(n log n)

3

θ(n2)

4

θ(log n)

✓ Correct option: 2
💡 View Explanation

In the D&C approach:

  1. Divide the array into two halves.
  2. Find majority M1 in left and M2 in right.
  3. To combine: If M1 or M2 exists, count their occurrences in the entire current range to see if one qualifies as the majority. This counting takes O(n) time.

Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).

By Master Theorem, this is T(n) = θ(n log n).

  • Note: While the Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm is O(n), the standard Divide & Conquer implementation is O(n log n).

❖ Question 580
UID: 5TMCR

Which of the following is/are TRUE?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

﻿Given an array A[1 . . n] of integers, the running time of Heap Sort is polynomial in the input size n.

2

Any n-node unbalanced tree can be balanced using O(log n) rotations.

3
✓ Correct Answer

AVL trees can be used to implement an optimal comparison-based sorting algorithm

4
✓ Correct Answer

Depth-first search will take Θ() time on a graph G = (V, E) represented as an adjacency matrix.-

✓ Correct option: 3, 4
💡 View Explanation

(a). Given an array A[1 . . n] of integers, the running time of Heap Sort is polynomial in the input size n. False. Counting Sort’s running time depends on the size of the numbers in the input, so it is pseudo-polynomial.


(b). Any n-node unbalanced tree can be balanced using O(log n) rotations. False. The worst-case unbalanced tree is a list, and balancing it requires Ω(n) rotations.


(c). AVL trees can be used to implement an optimal comparison-based sorting algorithm. True. AVL trees can be used to sort N numbers in O(N log N) time, by inserting all the numbers in the tree, and iteratively calling NEXT-LARGEST N times.


(d). Depth-first search will take Θ(V2) time on a graph G = (V, E) represented as an adjacency matrix. True. In this case, finding the neighbors of a vertex takes O(V ) time, which makes the total running time Θ(V2).

❖ Question 588
UID: KSK40

Let G = (V, E) be a directed acyclic graph (DAG). We want to find the longest path in G. Which of the following statements is true?

✓ Answer Available
1

The problem is NP-Hard for DAGs.

2

It5 can be solved in O(V+E) using a modified BFS.

3

❖ Question 599
UID: A3FBL

Consider the partitioning step of the Randomized QuickSort algorithm, where a pivot is chosen uniformly at random from the array of distinct elements, and the array is partitioned into two subarrays; elements less than the pivot go to the left subarray, and elements greater than the pivot go to the right subarray. The pivot itself is not included in either subarray.

Let the array have an odd length n=2k+1, and let the median be the (k+1)th smallest element.

What is the probability that the median element ends up in the right (second) half after partitioning?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

½

2

k/2k

3
✓ Correct Answer

k/ (2k+1)

4

1/(2k+1)

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

We are choosing the pivot uniformly at random from the n=2k+1 elements.

Let’s denote the median as the (k+1)th smallest element.

For the median to be placed in the right half (i.e., be greater than the pivot), the pivot must be one of the k smallest elements (elements smaller than the median).

  • Total elements: 2k+1
  • Probability that pivot is less than median = k/(2k+1)​
  • Because only in this case, the median will be placed in the right subarray (i.e., all greater elements than pivot go to right)

Hence, the correct probability is: k/(2k + 1)

❖ Question 608
UID: 7UD9S

Consider the given algorithm. Given an alphabet A with frequency distribution {f(a) : a ∈ A}. The binary Huffman tree is constructed using a priority queue, Q, of nodes, with labels (frequencies) as keys.


Huffman (A)

    {       n = |A|;

                Q = A;                               //the future leaves

                for i = 1 to n –1              

                { 

                   z = new node;

                   left[z] = Extract–min(Q);

                   right[z] = Extract – min (Q);

                   f[z] = f[left[z]] + f[right[z]];

                   Insert (Q, z);

         }

         return Extract – Min (Q)         //root of the tree

   {   

If each priority queue operation takes a time of O(log n), then what will be the running time of the given algorithm?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

O(n)

2

O (n2)

3
✓ Correct Answer

O (nlogn)

4

None of the above

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

Given:

  • Alphabet A has n characters.
  • Frequencies: {f(a) : a ∈ A}
  • A binary Huffman tree is constructed using a priority queue (min-heap).
  • Each operation on the priority queue takes O(log n) time.

 

Huffman Coding Algorithm Steps:

  1. Insert all n characters (as leaf nodes) into a min-heap.

     ⟶ Takes O(n) insertions × O(log n) per insertion = O(n log n)

      2. Repeat n - 1 times:

  • Remove the two nodes with the smallest frequencies.

     ⟶ Two extract-min operations = 2 × O(log n)

  • Create a new internal node with the sum of these two frequencies.
  • Insert the new node back into the heap.

   ⟶ One insert operation = O(log n)

So, each iteration takes O(log n) time and we repeat it n - 1 times

⟶ Total time = (n - 1) × O(log n) = O(n log n).

If the given sorting algorithm GATEsort is performed over an array A [] = {5, 3, 4, 2, 6, 1, 8, 9, 7, 0}, to sort the elements in ascending order.

❖ Question 610
UID: ZQ26H

In some situations, inserting an element into a MinHeap may take constant time, i.e., O(1).

Select all conditions where the insertion into a MinHeap takes O(1) time.

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

You are inserting the largest element into the heap

2

You are inserting the smallest element into the heap

3

The heap is perfectly balanced (equal number of left and right children for all nodes)

4

None of the above

✓ Correct option: 1
💡 View Explanation
  • In a MinHeap, the smallest element is at the root, and every parent is smaller than its children.
  • Insertion always starts by placing the new element at the bottommost-rightmost position and then percolating up if needed.

Option (a)

  • If you're inserting the largest element, it will be placed at the last position.
  • Since it’s larger than its parent, no percolation up is needed, and the insertion finishes in O(1) time.

 

Option (b)

  • If you're inserting the smallest element, it will need to percolate all the way up to the root.
  • This takes O(log n) time in the worst case.

 

Option (c)

  • The shape of the heap being balanced has no effect on whether insertion is O(1); time depends on value comparison, not structure.

 

Option (d)

  • Since option (a) is valid, "None of the above" is not correct.

❖ Question 617
UID: OW3XC

Consider a modified QuickSort where the pivot is always chosen as the element at the √n -th position in the sorted order of the current array of size n. What is the worst-case time complexity of this algorithm?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

O(n log n)

2

3

O(n2)

4

O(n log2 n)

✓ Correct option: 1
💡 View Explanation

Even though finding the exact √n-th smallest element might seem expensive, if we assume we have a pivot that splits the array into proportions of √n and n - √n, the recurrence relation is:

Since n - √n is still a very large fraction of n, this looks like a skewed split. However, the Master Theorem doesn't apply directly. Using a recursion tree, the depth is determined by how many times we can subtract approximately √n. But the question implies a rank-based pivot. If the pivot consistently provides a split where at least a constant fraction (like 1: 9 or even 1:√n) is maintained, we analyze the height. In this specific case, as long as the work at each level is O(n) and the subproblems eventually shrink, the "heavy" side of the recursion dominates. Actually, for any split where the subproblem is (n - nk) for k < 1, the complexity remains O(n log n) because the reduction is geometric in nature regarding the work done.

Why B & C are incorrect: These complexities arise from much worse splits (like constant size reductions) or significantly higher work per level.

1

Both Array and Single Linked List takes Θ(nlogn) time.

2

3

4

❖ Question 638
UID: MNEGA

Which of the following statements is true regarding the Divide and Conquer paradigm?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1
✓ Correct Answer

Divide and Conquer algorithms typically solve subproblems by merging solutions at the end, but the subproblems are not required to be of equal size.

2

Merge Sort is an example of a Divide and Conquer algorithm, where the "divide" step is not recursive.

3

The Divide and Conquer approach is generally less efficient than Dynamic Programming because it does not store intermediate results.

4

In Divide and Conquer, the problem is divided into subproblems of different types to simplify the original problem.

✓ Correct option: 1
💡 View Explanation

·Statement 1: True. Divide and Conquer algorithms work by dividing a problem into subproblems, solving each subproblem, and then combining their solutions. The subproblems do not have to be of equal size, though in some algorithms like Merge Sort, they often are.

·Statement 2: False. Merge Sort is indeed an example of a Divide and Conquer algorithm, but the "divide" step is recursive as it keeps splitting the array until single elements are left.

·Statement 3: False. Divide and Conquer can be more efficient than some methods, particularly when subproblems are independent. However, it is true that Dynamic Programming may be more efficient in cases where subproblems overlap and intermediate results need to be reused.

·Statement 4: False. In Divide and Conquer, the problem is divided into smaller subproblems of the same type, not different types, to simplify the original problem.

❖ Question 639
UID: ZX90I

You are given time measurements for a sorting method that uses an unknown sorting algorithm:

  • Sorting 1,000,000 identical elements takes 1 second
  • Sorting 2,000,000 identical elements takes 2 seconds
  • Sorting 100,000 distinct random elements takes 5 seconds
  • Sorting 200,000 distinct random elements takes 20 seconds

Based on this performance data, which sorting algorithm is most likely be used by this method?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

Quick Sort

2

Merge Sort

3
✓ Correct Answer

Insertion Sort

4

Selection Sort

✓ Correct option: 3
💡 View Explanation

For identical elements:

  • Insertion sort performs very well when the data is nearly sorted or has many repeated values.
  • Sorting 1M and 2M identical elements in linear time (O(n)) is consistent with insertion sort in best-case scenarios.

For random distinct elements:

  • Sorting 100K → 5 sec
  • Sorting 200K → 20 sec
  • Time quadruples when size doubles, suggesting O(n²) behaviour, which is typical for Insertion Sort in the worst case.

Other algorithms:

  • Merge Sort (O(n log n)) and Quick Sort (average O(n log n)) wouldn’t show such drastic increase in time.
  • Selection Sort has O(n²) for all inputs, but it performs the same on identical or random inputs—so it wouldn't be faster for identical elements.

Hence, the timing pattern best fits Insertion Sort.

❖ Question 657
UID: 8TCOZ

Which of the following statements is false regarding the Quick Sort algorithm?

Answer Options
✓ Answer Available
1

The worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort is O(n2) which occurs when the pivot selection is poor.

2

Quick Sort is an in-place sorting algorithm, meaning it requires only a small, constant amount of additional storage space.

3

﻿The average-case time complexity of Quick Sort is O(log n), making it efficient for most practical applications.

4

Quick Sort is a stable sorting algorithm, meaning it preserves the relative order of equal elements.

Option A: True. The worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort is O(n2). This occurs when the pivot selection leads to highly unbalanced partitions, such as always picking the smallest or largest element as the pivot.

Option B: True. Quick Sort is an in-place algorithm, meaning it does not require additional storage proportional to the size of the input (except for the recursion stack, which is typically O(log n)).


Option C: True. The average-case time complexity of Quick Sort is O(nlog n) which makes it efficient for sorting large datasets in most scenarios.

           

Option D: False. Quick Sort is not a stable sorting algorithm. The relative order of equal elements may not be preserved during the sorting process, depending on how the pivot is chosen and the implementation.
